utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case the IT-08-91-T, Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin by taking the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis along with Case Manager Jasmina Bosnjakovic for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm ready to proceed with our next witness, who is ST-159, Slobodan Markovic. While he's coming in, I would indicate to the Court with relation to one of the exhibits I propose to show this witness. It is tab 10 in the list I've sent around. It's Exhibit P1137 already in evidence, but in preparing I noticed that the English translation which is in e-court only has the first two pages. There's a third page that needs to be uploaded, and we're just seeking leave of the Court, if there's no objection from the Defence, to add that third page of the English translation and upload it into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, did I -- do I understand it's already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why -- the -- just a slight curiosity as to how it would have been exhibited with a missing page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the original B/C/S was complete, and in e-court it was simply the third page of the English translation inadvertently wasn't uploaded, only the first two pages. We've sent an e-mail to the Legal Officer and the Registry Officer indicating our desire to do that. And to the Defence as well. So it's merely -- I think it's merely just an administrative matter. I'm trying to make the record complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We had gotten communication that for the record the OTP was going to respond this morning to the application for provisional release of number one accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to advise the Court that the Prosecution does not intend to file anything in writing. I was asked to inform the Court of the Prosecution's general position opposing provisional release. However, at this stage of the case and given Mr. Stanisic's previous record, we take no position and leave it to the discretion of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. First of all, do you here me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read a solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Slobodan Markovic. I was born on the 14th of February, 1958, in Sarajevo, in what was then the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska as an inspector working war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was one of the managers in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, is this your first testimony before this Tribunal? Have you ever given testimony before, here or in any tribunal in your country on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I'm testifying before the Tribunal in The Hague. I have not given testimony anywhere. But on the 26th of February, 2008, your investigator, Mr. Barry from Canada, came to see me in my office in Bijeljina where I gave a statement to him. And there is a CD-ROM with a record of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me explain to you briefly how the proceedings will unfold here. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecutor, who is sitting on your right, and the Prosecutor has asked, all together, for three hours for your examination-in-chief. After that, counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting to your left, has asked for four hours. And Mr. -- the counsel for Mr. Zupljanin asked for two hours and a half to cross-examine you. When Mr. Pantelic, the counsel of Mr. Zupljanin is through, we will give the floor back to the Prosecutor who will have a chance to some final questions in light of the answers you have given to your cross-examination. And after that, and in between, the Judges may all -- may, at all times put questions to. After that, your testimony will be finished.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, one practical matter. Recordings here are taking on video-tape and the tapes have to be changed every 90 minutes. So that means that every hour and a half we have a break of about 20 minutes, and then we continue. The proceedings today will go from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00 and will resume tomorrow. That's all I have to say for the moment. Thank you very much. And I will give the floor now to Mr. Hannis for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I would indicate --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- at page 4, line 12, the witness gave an answer about being interviewed by an investigator, Mr. Barry from Canada. I would indicate that that is an investigator named Barry Hogan who works for the Office of the Prosecutor and not for the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I understand you're presently working for the MUP and you were working for the MUP in 1992. Can you tell us briefly when you first began working for the MUP and what education -- educational training you had before you began work there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I started working in the Ministry of the Interior of what was Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, I completed the Faculty for Physical Education in Sarajevo. And then for three and a half years I taught in a school. And later on I transferred to the police; that was on the 4th of August, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1991, where were you working and what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I worked in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo as an officer in charge of the operations centre in the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet and/or work with Mico Stanisic during that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At one time, Mr. Stanisic was my immediate superior as the chief of the centre there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what time-period that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in 1990, but I'm not entirely certain, because the chiefs of the centre came and went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about how in early April there was a split of the MUP in Bosnia, and a separate Serbian MUP or what later became called the Republika Srpska MUP was formed. Did there come a time when you left the old joint MUP and went to the Republika Srpska MUP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th of April, 1991, I left the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina because there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but your answer was translated as the 17th of April, 1991, and I believe that's probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, on 17th of April, I left the joint MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina because the situation in the security centre was such that that was great deal of animosity between the policemen of all three ethnicities, Serb, Croat, and Muslim. I left to join the training centre for the Ministry of Interior personnel in Vrace, in Sarajevo, where I joined the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you went to Vrace on the 17th of April, who -- who did you report to and what work did you begin doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, at the time, in Vrace, members of Serb ethnicity, employees of the police, were gathering there. My immediate superior was Mr. Cedo Kljajic, a man who used to work in the security centre before the war, and he was my immediate superior there, at that time. He was the head of the police there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say Cedo Kljajic was the head of the police there, did you mean in Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the police in the public security centre in Sarajevo before the war and then he held the same post, like the police chief, because, at that time, posts were being established in the new Ministry of the Interior of what was then the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in Vrace until the 9th of May, 1992, and then I left for Pale at the recommendation of Mr. Cedo Kljajic, who knew me as an employee of his, and he recommended me to be a member of the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoner, representing the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's me show you an exhibit that's in evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is P179.18. It's at tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It will be up on the screen in a minute, Mr. Markovic? This is dated the 8th May, 1992, and it's entitled: "A Decision to Form a Central Commission." And the name of Slobodan Markovic appears at number 2 as a representative of the Ministry of the Interior for the Central Commission. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of this decision in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received it immediately when I arrived in Pale on the 9th of May. As can you see, the decision was issued by the prime minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Professor Branko Djeric, on the 8th of May. So I arrived there one day after this decision on the establishment of the Central Commission was issued, and I received a copy of this decision. I have a copy myself, but it had been faxed to me so it's now virtually illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you went to Pale on the 9th of May, how did it come about that you were named to join this commission? Did Mr. Kljajic ask to you volunteer, or had he already put your name in and he was just telling you that you were going there? What do you know about that? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already noted that Mr. Cedo Kljajic had been my superior officer in the joint Ministry of Interior in the security centre in the police department to which I belonged. He had known me for a number of years and probably appreciated my knowledge and experience. He asked me if I would like to go to Pale and be a member of the Central Commission representing the MUP. I asked him, perhaps a bit inappropriately, how long that would last. And he told me, Well, some 15 or 20 days. He obviously didn't think that it -- there would be chaos in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it would last for much, much longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you actually end up working for the commission for exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until the end of March 1993. On the 1st of April of 1993, I transferred to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina where an office was set up, and I worked as an inspector there in the Police Department of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The other members of the commission named in this decision - I see from our copy on the screen that it's a pretty poor copy - but I understand from other evidence that number 1 is Rajko Colovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Rajko Colovic is represented under number 1. He represented the Ministry of Justice and Administration of Republika Srpska, and he also was the chairman of the commission, because the commission worked under the auspices of the justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number three is a Lieutenant-Colonel Caslav Mihajlovic. Did you ever see him? Did he ever come and do any work on the commission that you know of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant-Colonel Mihajlovic, Caslav is listed under number 3. He represented the Ministry of National Defence, and he was also a member of the Central Commission. But this gentleman never appeared, and I never actually got introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sometime later on in 1992 was there another individual who came to represent the Ministry of Defence or the army on the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that there was a serious gentleman. I think he was colonel or lieutenant-colonel; a high-ranking officer at any rate. His name was Budimir Djordjic. But he stayed there for just one day, he got acquainted with the work of the ministry, and then he never showed up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after him, anyone else from the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No one from the Defence Ministry ever worked in the commission as a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or how about the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, there was Mr. Dragan Bulajic. Months later. He represented the army there in the commission. But that was later on. After several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. And how long did Mr. Colovic remain in the position of president of the commission, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we started working on the 9th of May. I think that sometime on the 6th of June, 1992, he asked the prime minister to be allowed to leave the commission, because he was a lawyer, a judge, and probably this was not the job to his liking. He was probably looking for a better job, keeping in sight his career. And there was an opening somewhere for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of your job, when you went to work for this government-created commission for exchange of prisoners, what was your relationship with the MUP? Were you still an employee of MUP during this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was still an employee of the Ministry of the Interior, and they paid my salary, paltry as it was; but as a representative of the Ministry of the Interior, I sat there on this commission, which was part of the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, in connection with that, an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 65 ter 1271 [Realtime transcript read in error "1275"]. This is tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, coming up on the screen in a moment will be what appears to be a payroll list or sheet for the MUP in connection with September 1992. And do you see number 18 on that list on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your title is -- your job duty or description is as an inspector. Were you still working on the Exchange Commission in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was working on the Exchange Commission, and as I told you, I was being paid by my -- by the Ministry of the Interior. We were not paid by the government. I was being paid by the MUP as an inspector with a university education, as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1487, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see in the transcript at page 11, line 13, it was indicated as 65 ter Exhibit "1275," and it should be "1271," just to be clear. And that is the one that's on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markovic, when you began your work for the commission, did you have any kind of guidance or direction from the prime minister or anyone else about what you were supposed to do in the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Only one of the people working in the government secretariat. I think he was a secretary in the cabinet. I think his name was Nedeljko Lakic. When we were chatting informally, he told me we would be given an office in Kalovita Brda in a hotel called Buducnost and that there we would be receiving parties, conducting conversations or talks, and so on. So that was all the information I got, and I got it from Mr. Lakic. No one expected that it would last as long as it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you given any marching orders about how you were supposed to go about your job, or did you and Mr. Colovic figure out on your own what you were going to do and how you were going to do it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Pale and when the commission was established, people heard that there was a Commission for Exchange. And on both sides -- members of both sides were brought, and we had a conversation with a member of the BH commission about exchanges. And these were carried out at the demarcation line between Sarajevo and Pale. I think the gentleman's name was Musir Brkic, on the other side, the Bosnian side, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you next a document that is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P427.7. It's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up, Mr. Markovic, I'll tell you it's dated the 6th of June, 1992, and it has the name of Rajko Colovic as president of the commission and a signature at the bottom of the last page. It's entitled an order. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Rajko Colovic and I drew this document up together, but it was he who signed it, as president of the commission. I remember this well. Here we prescribed the way prisoners were to be treated, civilians, soldiers, and so on, and can you see this from the order itself, the manner in which the premises should be arranged, what they should contain, sanitary facilities, and so on and so forth. Can you see all this from the document, that they should be allowed to receive food, clothes, items of personal hygiene, even food brought by their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the order in the first paragraph we see that all the public security services are supposed to keep records of persons detained or brought in. And in the second paragraph: That they shall submit lists of detainees or persons deprived of liberty to municipal commissions for exchange. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the public security service had the right to detain persons up to three days on their premises. They could not deprive them of their liberty but they could detain them. After that, the persons detained on these premises at the Security Services Centres were handed over to members of the Army of Republika Srpska. And from that point onwards, it was the army who took over all responsibility for these people, including housing, food, clothing, and so on. So the employees of the Security Services Centre could only detain people for up to three days. After that, they had to hand them over to members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that's how the law and the regulations were written. But, in fact, are you aware that sometimes people were detained by members of the MUP for more than three days during 1992? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at that time, I was at Pale. I'm not saying these things did not happen in some places controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska without out knowledge. At that time, there were no telephone or teleprinter communications, and the roads were bad, and it's possible that such things did occur. However, at Pale, where I was employed, I can tell you that no such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One -- one thing in your previous answer that maybe you can help me with, and I think it may be a matter of translation or the difference between the Serbian and English languages. At page 14, line 8, your answer, you said: "Members of the public security service had the right to detain persons up to three days on their premises. They could not deprive them of their liberty but they could detain them." Can you explain for me what is the difference between detaining someone and depriving someone of their liberty? Because, for me, in English, detention is a form of depriving someone of their liberty. So I think maybe it's a technical term that means something different in Serbian. If you could, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, detention or detaining someone is when you, for example, find someone drunk driving and you detain them until they sober up. That is a form of detention. A person found drunk driving, regardless of whether they have caused the traffic accident or not, is detained on the premises until they sober up. Also, persons who committed crimes, regardless of ethnicity, whether they were citizens of Serb ethnicity or non-Serb ethnicity, could be detained up to three days. After that, they had to be taken to the district court, and the district court would proceed further and take further action. And then they might be sent to a remand prison or whatever. So it was up to the court to decide what to do with them in connection with the crime they committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and what was depriving someone of their liberty mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, depriving someone of their liberty is a completely different thing from detention. A person can be deprived of his or her liberty if they have committed a serious crime and if it is thought they might repeat that crime. Then they are deprived of their liberty. If it's thought that if released they might influence witnesses who could testify in their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the second page of the B/C/S and the last page of the English of this document on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I see that this document was sent to several addressees, including the Ministry of Justice, the MUP, the -- the centres, and the public security stations, as well as regional and municipal commissions for exchange. Do you know, as of early June 1992, how many regional and municipal commissions for exchange were in existence, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say what number was existence, because the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities organised their own commissions for the exchange of prisoners, and we were unable to send them proper instructions because the regional staffs established these commissions and exchanged Serbs for Muslims. And when you say that this was addressed to all, I don't know whether the commissions received this document at all or whether the municipal and regional commissions and the public security stations received it. I doubt that teleprinters, faxes, and so on were working at the time. They were not operational. So they acted according to the instructions of these War Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could show you next an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: P228 in evidence. This is tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a -- these are the minutes of a government meeting on the 9th of June, 1992. I think you've -- you saw this one during proofing.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't see it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And item number 1 (a) on the agenda is the Order of the Central Committee for the Exchange of Prisoners. Is that the document we were just looking at, the one signed by Mr. Colovic that you and he prepared together?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't sign it, but we did draw it up together. He was the only one who signed it. But yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page we see that the government has supported the order of the Central Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says the government acknowledged the letter of correspondence from the president of the Central Committee for Exchange, and it's been concluded that the minister of justice should talk to Rajko Colovic, the committee president, to determine what are the motives for requesting the change. Do you know what's that -- what that is about? What change was Mr. Colovic requesting around the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, Mr. Colovic may have thought that it was beneath his dignity as a judge from the previous system, that he deserved a better job. He was young, he had great career prospects, and he thought he could do better. And that's why they were looking for someone else to fill his place on the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not he was replaced; and, if so, who replaced him, as president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Much later on, a member of the commission turned up with two colleagues from the Ministry of Justice who were drawing up lists and talking to members of the public. And a man called Nenad Vanovac turned up and introduced himself as the new president of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War. I said I'm glad to meet you, I'm glad we'll be cooperating. He spent that day at Pale and then he went back to Ilidza Brigade, from where he had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. I don't think that the beginning of the answer, the witness's answer, was recorded as witness said. So it's page 18, line 7, 8, and 9. I believe he was talking about the fact that he was sitting in the -- in the office with two members of the Ministry of Justice. Maybe you can clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- you heard what Mr. Zecevic said. Our English translation in the transcript says your answer was: "Much later on, a member of the commission turned up with two colleagues from the Ministry of Justice who were drawing up lists ..." Was that yourself you were referring to as the member of the commission who was drawing up lists with --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- two members? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, I'm afraid the gentleman didn't understand me. When Rajko Colovic left, two young women from the Ministry of Justice arrived. They did administrative work. They collected lists. People arrived in our office in Pale to report missing persons. They said their sons or brothers had gone missing on the line. They were employees of the Ministry of Justice, but they were not members of the commission. They were simply administrative staff, two girls. One was called Biljana Brkic; today she is a judge or a lawyer in Doboj. The other one is called Gordana Bagic [phoen], and I don't know where she is today. She typed out those lists. She didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who replaced Mr. Colovic as a representative of the Ministry of Justice and took up the position of president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that a person called Nenad Vanovac turned up. He came from Ilidza, which is a suburb of Sarajevo. And at that time it was being held by members of the Army of Republika Srpska. He introduced himself as the new president of the commission and said he had been appointed by the minister of justice, Mr. Momcilo Mandic. I introduced myself. He didn't show me any documents, any decision or letter. I accepted his word. We discussed the lists, the problems on the ground, the fact that the other side was not respecting our mutual agreements, that they were not bringing the number of people we asked for or the people we asked for by name. I told him all this, and after that, he went back to Ilidza. Probably he worked in that part of Sarajevo on these exchanges, and I remained with those two young women I mentioned who were doing administrative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Vanovac then do any work together, or was he working separately in Ilidza and you were working in Pale, sort of doing your own thing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with the best will in the world to cooperate, it was not possible. There were no telephone lines, no teleprinter communications, all the roads from Pale to the other part of Sarajevo were blocked. It was impossible to reach Ilidza at the time, to meet or to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you, regarding Mr. Vanovac, Exhibit P1137.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the usher's help, if I could hand him a hard copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, while this is coming up, I'll tell you it's a transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation dated the 23rd of June, 1992, between a Nenad Vanovac and Momcilo Mandic. At the bottom of your first page, I think, and at the top of the second page in English, Mr. Vanovac ask: "Who am I going to be talking to in the future? I can't find this Elez anywhere." Mandic says: "Forget Elez. Everything's here with me directly until I find the right man." Do you know who the Elez is that's being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Elez was a lower-ranking officer of the Army of Republika Srpska. He had some sort of rank, but I don't remember exactly, a sergeant or something like that. He was representing the army. He was trying to manipulate something through civilians, but he was never a member of the commission established by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any work to do with the exchange of prisoners on behalf of the military, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He had nothing to do with the work of the official Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, the state commission. He nothing to do with it. And he was not a member of that commission. He was with the army, he carried military insignia, he did not have any decision appointing him to the commission, and he had had nothing to do with the Central Commission by the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the next page in your B/C/S, you see there's mention of Rajko Colovic. And then, further on, Mr. Vanovac says: "They called me about the eight you approve for the exchange with Hrasnica and Kolonija. This seems like Mr. Mandic's approved an exchange of prisoners." Am I reading that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. Mr. Mandic, as the ministry of justice, was the superior of all the prison wardens belonging to the Ministry of Justice. How this was done and what they actually were doing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could look next at Exhibit P1318.25. It's at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this will be on your screen in a moment. It's dated the 4th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's a document from the minister of justice, signed by someone else but signed for Momcilo Mandic. And you see it's informing that Mr. Nenad Vanovac has been appointed president of the Central Commission for Exchange of Prisoners -- or prison soldiers and individuals.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see, in the last line: "The decision by the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be forwarded subsequently." So the minister of justice is appointing him, but the decision will be forwarded subsequently. I have to say that the first time I saw this document was during the proofing yesterday. Although he had already introduced himself to me as the president and I accepted his word, you see he was appointed by Momcilo Mandic himself, the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, now, a little bit about how your day-to-day work functioned on the commission. And let me show you, in connection with that, Exhibit P179.17. This is tab 2 in the binder. I think you said you arrived Pale on the 9th of May. And this document has a date of 14 May, so it seems to one of your earliest involvements in exchanges or dealing with prisoners or detained persons.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is my handwriting. I wrote this. 400 persons on 18 pages who were brought from Bratunac to Pale. This is my handwriting on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we look at page 3 of the B/C/S and of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that your signature in the handwritten entry at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says here: "Member of the government commission on behalf of the Serbian MUP for the exchange of prisoners of war, Slobodan Markovic." And you can see my signature in the bottom right-hand corner, and the date is there in the bottom left-hand corner. But the lists are not in my handwriting. It was probably those two secretaries, those two female colleagues, who actually wrote the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm sorry. Just -- if I can just make a note there. On page 21, line 19, the -- the witness's answer was recorded as a part of your question. Thank you. The answer starts after "the imprisoned soldiers." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, concerning this group of 400 or so men from Bratunac, how -- how did you become involved in this? How did you find out they were there, and how did you get involved in doing anything in connection with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by a person from the communications centre in the Army of Republika Srpska that 400 people had arrived from Bratunac, escorted by the military police and the army. As Rajko Colovic, at that time, was not in Pale, and he was still a member of the commission at the time, he was at Han Pijesak which is some 60 or so kilometres away or more from Pale, I went to fetch him as the president. I went to fetch him from his home and brought him back to Pale. In the meantime, all these people who had been brought from Bratunac were put in the gym of the primary school in Pale. Some were in civilian clothes. A good part wore parts of uniforms, military uniforms. Some had olive-drab JNA shirts. Some had military boots or military pants and so on. And there were also some individuals who were dressed in civilian clothes without any parts of military uniform. But most of them did have at least one item of clothing that was a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you speak with any of these men detained at the Pale elementary school gym?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: When food was distributed to them, they came in the evening and left the next day, but they were served three meals. And I would like to say that we gave them some fish with bread because we didn't want to given them meat because we were afraid that they would not want to eat it because of their religious beliefs. We respected those religious beliefs and gave them some fish. We spoke to the representatives of those people, and they asked what would happen to them. I had already been told that all 400 of them would be transferred to Visoko. So people were free to move. And all 400 of them were to be taken to Visoko, to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And, later on, this was confirmed by a document sent by Nedin Vranac [phoen], the head of the police station in Visoko, who thanked us for our actions and for the fact that those people had not been maltreated in any way. They had simply been taken there on three or four -- two or three trailer trucks to the demarcation line under military escort where they were taken in by the forces of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In part of your answer, you said, line 3, page 24: "I had already been told that all 400 of them would be transferred to Visoko." Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this had been arranged. This was a huge number of people. 400 people. In Pale, there were people who had lost their kin, their brothers, children, and so on, in the fighting, and it was very difficult to keep the 400 safe from those Serbs who had lost their family members. They were guarded by the military police, and it was arranged that they would be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was agreed with the prime minister that they would be moved to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Colovic had probably spoken to the prime minister. As the chairman of the commission, he got in touch with the prime minister and then the prime minister spoke to the Crisis Staff, as I could see from your documents, the Crisis Staff in Sokolac. And he asked them to provide three trailer trucks to transport those ethnic Muslims to Visoko. Although it was logical for the prime minister to notify us as the Central Commission, representing his and our function, and we were supposed to take over from that time because it was not logical for the prime minister to ask the Sokolac Crisis Staff to provide the trucks, because we could have done the same thing. We -- it was really our job to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said in the previous answer that these men were guarded by the military police. At the elementary school in Pale, weren't there also some regular police guarding them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Sir, I did not say it was in the elementary school. It was in the gym of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And weren't there also regular police guarding them as well as military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the security was provided by the military police and the Republika Srpska army troops. They secured the building. But it was also a fact that in the immediate vicinity of this building there was the public security station in Pale, and it is quite possible that some police officers would come and speak to their colleagues from the army, and it might have appeared that they also had been involved in guarding the building but that was not the case. They did their job, the job of the operatives of the Ministry of Interior. They were there on their regular business, as far as it could be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying you didn't see any regular police inside the gymnasium of the elementary school during the time these 400 prisoners were kept there in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In the gym where they were detained? No. Regular police did not enter those premises. I was the only one who got in, in order to speak to their representatives, to tell them that everything would be all right, that there should not be concern, and that they would be transferred to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a minute. Let me ask you about your work in -- in dealing with exchanges with the other side. Did you know an individual named Amor Masovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Masovic. Amor Masovic. He was a chairman of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And today he actually chairs the institute for the search for the missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On all sides. They search for the missing people in all the ethnic communities. It's a central institute; it was established in Sarajevo. But, yes, I had heard about him, and I did meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the two of you work together with a list that each of you had of detained individuals in the other person's territory? For example, did you have list of Serbs you believed were being detained in Mr. Masovic's part of the territory, and did he have list of non-Serbs that he believed were being detained in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Practically every other day I went to Lukavica from Pale - That's in eastern Sarajevo as it is now - where I was met by an APC, an SFOR or UNPROFOR APC. I don't know what it was called. I think it was SFOR. So we would drive to Lukavica in our own car. We would transfer to the SFOR APC. And there were two other APCs providing security. We would be in the middle, and we would go to attend talks at the Sarajevo airport. And the people from Sarajevo, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, would arrive in Sarajevo in the same manner, and we would sit down in a special room where we would hold our meetings, exchange lists, arrange dates for the exchanges, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Colovic or Mr. Vanovac ever participate with you in these kind of meetings with Mr. Masovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Colovic never showed up. Colovic had already left the commission by that time. And Mr. Vanovac was in Ilidza, so he was not in touch with them at all. And only I and Amor Masovic arranged those meetings. And when we met, we would agree on the next meeting. Because it was impossible, we didn't have any telephone lines, so we would agree to meet in two days at the same place. And we had to arrange our meetings in that way because the telephone lines were down and there were no telefaxes so we had to bring the list to those meetings and exchange them to arrange for the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And related to the exchanges, can you tell us about the principle that's referred to as the all-for-all principle in connection with exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The principle all for all was agreed, but the other side did not respect it. And this principle means that if, for instance, our side has, let's say, 20 Muslims in captivity and the other side has 70 Serbs, Serb prisoners, they should exchange -- they should be exchanged all for all: 20 for 70. So it's not ten for ten; it's all for all, regardless of how many you have on one side you exchange them for all the prisoners on the other side, regardless of how many there are. Especially when it comes to the civilians because it was more a question of the flow of the population, the free movement of the population, allowing the people to decide where they wanted to live, on what territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I am sure you are correct that sometimes the other side did not respect the all-for-all. But are aware of occasions where the Serb side did not respect the all-for-all principle in exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On our side, what I did at the demarcation line near Sarajevo and Pale it was not the case. But I am -- cannot be certain about other parts of Republika Srpska because I was not there. Because I did not have any contact with Banja Luka, with Doboj, Brod, or any other places held by our people. We did not have telephones, and it was only later that we were able to establish telephone lines and have telephone numbers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know an individual named Filip Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw him. I only know that this gentleman had been working in the socialist system before the war, and I heard of him in that capacity. I never met him. But, for a while, he was the president of the State Commission of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the Exchange of Prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me -- and he was a Serb by ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit P1318.24. This is tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Markovic, this is a document that, some time in late June 1992, there's a fax header on the B/C/S copy which has not been noted in the English translation, but the date at the upper left of the original B/C/S seems to be 26 June 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the body of the document, it makes reference to something having been received on the 22nd of June. I will tell you - we'll look at it in a minute - but I will tell you that this is from Filip Vukovic whose stamp and signature appear on the last page. It's to the Central Commission for Exchange of Persons. Do you recall ever seeing this document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. And this was not the fax message that I had in 1992. Now, in the upper part, you can see where the fax was sent from. It was from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the lower fax, in the left-hand corner, that's not my fax, where it says the Commission of the Exchange of Prisoners. It might be the justice ministry fax. Well, you have a list. You have my fax number and my telephone number and the telephone numbers of the other commissions. I have never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The fax 785 025 is the one that you say might be a Ministry of Justice number in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Might be. I am not saying that it is. But since we were under their auspices, it might well be their fax. And I never saw this fax. We didn't receive it. And you can see the Brijesce, Ilidza of Vrbanja Most are mentioned here. These are parts that belong to Mr. Vanovac. Brijesce and Ilidza, they were under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you'll see in that first paragraph that Mr. Vukovic is complaining about a recent exchange, where he says that his side released all the persons agreed, but of the agreed 45 on the Serb side, only seven were released. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Because -- I'm sorry. I really don't know who he wrote this to. Because I have never seen this document. Whether this is addressed to Vanovac or what, the date, just a moment, it's the 12th ... 12th or the 18th of June. No, I really don't have any idea what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the third page of the English and the second page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a name I want to point out to you. You see Roman numeral IV: Persons arrested in Ilidza on 14 May whose exchange has been arranged. And number one is a Bucan, Anes. Anes Bucan. Do you see that name?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Anes Bucan, number one. That's the only --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... remember that name for a little while. I'm going show you another document in a minute, but I'm going to finish with this one first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the last -- if we could go to the last page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It makes a reference to an attachment with a list of prisoners from 1 through 3.441. Did you ever see such a list from Mr. Masovic or anyone else on the other side in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted]. I am unfamiliar with this figure. It is a huge number of people. I have never seen this document. And you can see that Filip Vukovic signed it as the chairman of the state commission of the federal commission, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At the top of the page in that big paragraph near the bottom of it, he says - and the English actually starts on the preceding page - he says: "The attachment contains the list of imprisoned persons and detainees according to our records. It is our opinion that once released the detainees should be sent to their places of residence, that is, to their domicile address, otherwise this would signify typical deportation, exile, and ethnic cleansing of the area. Such persons should also be issued with appropriate certificates to prevent arrests for the second or third time." Were aware of this position being taken by Mr. Vukovic apparently on behalf of the other side, that if you release people only to send them out of the territory it was -- it would be viewed as deportation, exile, and ethnic cleansing? Was that something that was ever discussed in your presence in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to repeat that I have never seen this document by Mr. Filip Vukovic. And now, if you are asking me if it's deportation, no it's not; it's just a freedom of movement of the citizens, because people wanted to cross over to the territory where their fellow people from their ethnic community lived. But the problem is that they had to cross our lines in order to enter the territory of the Federation. And sometimes it was impossible to reach the Federation lines because of the lay of the land. And that's not deportation; it's just allowing people freedom of movement. People who wanted to move. I didn't want to live in Sarajevo. I had lived in Sarajevo for 34 years, yet I left it. I left everything behind and I moved to the territory of Republika Srpska. Well, it was not exactly what you would call the freedom of movement. I barely got out alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move to a different topic. I know it's a minute or two early, but can we take the first break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, I understand we had a correction to make about an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to correct for the record 65 ter 1271 was assigned in error, number P1487. And, instead, 65 ter 1271 becomes Exhibit P1501. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we've seen that in connection with the work of exchanging prisoners and detained persons that although you were on the Central Commission, which was created by the government, that exchanges were being conducted by other -- other groups and other individuals, such as regional or municipal commissions, and individuals like Mr. Mandic, as minister of justice. Were you aware that there were other -- other private or --or separate individuals that were trying to make their own arrangements for exchange of prisoners and detained persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know them personally. I mentioned Mr. Elez a little while ago. I don't know what his position was. I don't know. Perhaps he represented the Republika Srpska army. But those commissions that were established at the municipal level, they were established by the War Staffs in the municipalities. They were authorised to set up their own commissions in order to deal with the exchanges of prisoners, their prisoners for the detained Muslims. And that was not under the auspices of this official commission of the Republika Srpska government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It seems to me that all of this made your job extra difficult, because you're on the Central Commission for Exchange, but exchanges are going on all the time without you being informed. Did that make your job harder than it needed to be?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it was really a thankless job, working in the commission where you have 20 or 30 persons who would come to see you daily. Their family members, their sons had been killed or massacred, mutilated, gone missing in the fighting, and they wanted us to find at least one body part for them to be able to bury. And it was really difficulty because we didn't have any means of communication, telephones, a even it was impossible to use the roads to take -- to go to those places in other parts of Republika Srpska where those commissions were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P1228; this is tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could, with the usher's help, hand a hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Markovic, this will be with you in a moment. It's another transcript of an intercepted telephone conversation. And this one is dated 25 June 1992. The primary speakers are Momcilo Krajisnik and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't recall, did you have a chance to look at this one during proofing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, you showed me this document yesterday during the proofing session, which was why I was here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you follow on, you will see that Mr. Krajisnik is informing Mr. Mandic about a Dusan Savic who is the brother of a Milo Savic and that Dusan's been arrested and he's asking Mr. Mandic's help to see if that person can be located on the other side and exchanged or released. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday was the first time that I saw this document, when you showed me, and I had never heard the name Dusan Savic before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, I understand. I just want to confirm that that conversation is about trying to locate and arrange the exchange or release of a Dusan Savic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can see that Mr. Momcilo Mandic, as the justice minister, did have this capability. He was actually able to do that. It was probably a friend of theirs, and I had never met him. I'm unfamiliar with the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you, related to that, another phone conversation the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's Exhibit P1134.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could hand you a hard copy of that one. I will trade you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What is the tab number? Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That is tab number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This one is the following day, the 26th of June, 1992, between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Mandic. On the second page of the English at the bottom of the page, and for you I think it's the third page of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik is following up and asking about: "Let me also ask you, what about this Savic, Milos, since it's his brother?" And his brother, as we saw before, is Dusan. And Mr. Mandic says: "President, I put it on the list. The first next exchange and it will be finished." When you were working as a member of the exchange commission, did you ever see any list from Mr. Mandic of persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I really did not see that at all. And I never actually received it. There this was not addressed to me. Because this was absolutely done bypassing the official commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you follow on immediately from that part - and it's page 3 of the English - you see that Mr. Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik have some discussion about Filip Vukovic and his role on the exchange commission on the other side and his -- his claim that what the Serbs were doing in letting the women and children go to Vrbanja was ethnic cleansing. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that they were all released across -- to go across the Vrbanja Most bridge, which was in the centre of the city itself in the immediate vicinity of the city centre, I -- that was just the freedom of movement of population. They could decide where they wanted to live. Because they were a problem to us, if I may put it that way, and they were also a problem to the territory where they were heading to. So we were trying to solve our problem but in a normal, humane way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Let me show you, next, Exhibit P1157. This is tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, if could I have the usher's help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more intercepted telephone conversation. And this one, Mr. Markovic, is dated the 1st of July. This time it's between Mr. Mandic and Radovan Karadzic. And let me see if I can find the right page. Do you see where Mr. Mandic informs that they're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Yes. About five lines down below that, Mr. Mandic says: "We have many on the list. There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims who have been kept here for seven days. No one has inquired about them. No one seems to care. I don't know what to do." And then he goes on to say: "We'll try to exchange them for people from Hrasnica."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica is a part of Sarajevo, but it's on the outskirts. There were large industrial facilities there, and many Serbs were employed in Hrasnica but also a large number of Muslims. At the very outset when the war broke out, the Muslims managed to take Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija and then they tried to exchange those people. I don't know about this conversation. And how could I, because it's a conversation between the prime minister and the minister of justice, and it's an intercept. So how could I know about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Your answer was translated as "a conversation between the prime minister and the minister of justice." I -- perhaps you were misinterpreted, but Mr. Karadzic was the president of the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the republic, yes. The Radovan Karadzic, the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that the transcript was correct. Thank you. And then Mr. Karadzic goes on and was asking Mr. Mandic if he had found a particular Croat in Kula, and Mr. Mandic informs him that all the Croats have already been exchanged. Were you involved in any exchanges of Croats, or only Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Only Muslims. On the territory of Sarajevo, there was a very small percentage of Croats, and now they amount to about 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I think I have one more telephone conversation I want to show you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, again, if could I have the usher's help. This is Exhibit P1229, and it's tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was dated the 12th of August, 1992. Let me start by asking you if you knew a person by the name of Fahrija Karkin.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally. I saw him on television. But before the fighting broke out in Sarajevo, I heard that he was one of the better lawyers. And I think that in these criminal proceedings he was co-counsel for Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mirko Krajisnik; do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I've heard of him. I know he's Momcilo Krajisnik's brother. But I don't know him personally. I have heard of him. And I have heard that he is Momcilo Krajisnik's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Karkin, what -- what ethnicity was he; if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim. Then they were called Muslims; now they are called Bosniaks again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You will see there's a long decision between Mirko Krajisnik and Mr. Karkin about an exchange they're trying to arrange. On page 2 of the English and page -- I believe it's also page 2 of your B/C/S, yes. One of the persons to be included in this exchange is Dusan Savic. Do you remember that name we saw earlier in the phone conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I'm not familiar with this document. Even the names mentioned here, Kokot, Grujic, Skobalj, are names I have never heard before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But you see the name Dusan Savic near the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S as one of the persons being discussed for this exchange that Mr. Mirko Krajisnik and Mr. Karkin are trying to arrange?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, again, I take it that this is -- this is not an exchange that you were informed about or involved in, in your role as member of the Central Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What -- what position, if any, did Mirko Krajisnik have in -- in the government or the police or the Ministry of Justice in August of 1992; if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Did he hold any position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Momcilo and his brother, yes, he was the president of the Assembly. But Mirko Krajisnik, as far as I know, was never a member of the government or held any official post. I think he was engaged in private business, a private enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to show you Exhibit P1475.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is tab number 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is just a short one-page document, Mr. Markovic, and we'll put it up on the screen for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated the 30th of August, 1992. It appears to be from the minister Mico Stanisic with a stamp and signature, addressed to the administration of the Kula Prison, Ministry of Justice, Commission for Exchange of Detainees. And it says: "We hereby ask you to ensure the release of the prisoner Anes Bucan." Do you remember that name we saw before in the 26th June --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The name was mentioned just a while ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was in the 26th June document from Filip Vukovic. In --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In August 1992, you were still working for the Exchange Commission. Did Minister Stanisic know that you were working for this Exchange Commission from May 1992 throughout the rest of the year? Was he aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he knew I worked in that commission but not the period of time that I worked in it. Because we happened to run into each other on two occasions where I had my office, and he asked me, How are the exchanges going? Can you reach agreement with them? And I simply told him that they were refusing to respect the lists we had agreed on at the meetings. And he gave me some instructions, that the prisoners should be treated in line with the Geneva Conventions, that especially women and young children were not to be maltreated, and that exchanges should be carried out in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, and that their accommodation should be in compliance wherever possible, even though it all came under the Ministry of Justice and the VRS. And if I may say, where Mico Stanisic, the minister of the interior, is writing to the management of the Kula Prison, the Ministry of Justice, and he says: please allow the prisoners to be released. Look at that level, the rank; the minister, in fact, is not ordering the prison warden, or demanding and requesting, but asking him, pleading with him. He says, please allow prisoner Anes Bucan to be released and exchanged for three Serb families, which shows that he was not competent, he actually wasn’t. Because had the minister of the interior been competent, he would have had it done, absolutely. But he, the minister, was actually asking the prison warden, someone who was far below him in rank, for the exchange to take place. I think this makes everything clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. The part of the answer which witness gave on page 40 when he was talking to Mr. Stanisic was not recorded. The last part of the answer. Maybe the witness was talking too fast and the interpreters were not able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hannis, where are we heading with all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's something I would rather not discuss in front of the witness, if -- if we need to have the discussion. Maybe I can ask him a few additional questions, and you'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, carry on for the moment, but see if you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- help the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As far as Mr. Zecevic's point, I would simply ask him to try and address it on cross-examination, because that was such a long answer, I don't know where to begin to try and find what was omitted. And, frankly, it was non-responsive -- much of it was non-responsive to my specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: One of the points which Mr. Zecevic made which bears repeating is -- and I'm speaking -- I would address the witness directly. Please, sir, bear in mind that your evidence has to be interpreted so that you -- you need to remind yourself to slow down in giving your answers so that we have an accurate record of what you intend to convey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for telling me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I take it that Minister Stanisic didn't speak to you as a member of the commission about Anes Bucan, and didn't involve you in trying to facilitate this proposed exchange?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he never mentioned that name to me. We spoke only about the way exchanges were being carried out and so on. But no names were mentioned by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though he knew you were a member of the Exchange Commission and that you were an employee of the MUP, his ministry. Wouldn't it seem logical that he would speak to you about such a matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it would seem logical, but he had already sent that document to the Ministry of Justice which was supposed to deliver it to me, and the commission was supposed to deal with it further. But I never received this document from the Ministry of Justice, the document signed by Minister Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we saw from the 26th June fax from Mr. Vukovic that Anes Bucan had been arrested on 14th of May. So apparently by the end of August he is still being held, which is much more than the three days; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, not more than three days. But he was in Kula Prison. It was an official prison before the war, during the war, and after the war. It's still in existence. Whether Anes Bucan was there as a prisoner of war or as a person suspected of committing a serious crime and awaiting trial, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. I'd like to show you, next, Exhibit P192, which is at tab 26. This is a document dated the 8th of August, 1992. It's from the deputy minister for police affairs, Tomo Kovac, addressed to the president of the Republic and to the prime minister. Had you ever seen this document before you -- you came for proofing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see on the first page, the second paragraph, the second sentence, Mr. Kovac says: "There are cases where MUP members accept or in some cases even take part in capturing people in the war zones. After that, they arrange accommodation for them and a way of life, they determine the duration of their detention and their entire destiny." Were you aware of this fact that is purported to be by Mr. Kovac about MUP's involvement in capturing or accepting some of the people captured in war zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: If the members of the MUP were in the war areas, they were under the authority of the Army of Republika Srpska. When they became attached to the army, they were under the authority of the Army of Republika Srpska, and then they were soldiers, not policemen, and the military controlled them. Everything was under military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The moment they came to be in the area where there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think apart from your -- your visit to the primary school gymnasium in Pale in mid-May in connection with the 400 men from Bratunac, I understand --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- you did not visit any other camps or detention facilities during 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In late October, as I told you, and we'll come to that, I visited the camp in Manjaca, when I tried to organise an exchange at a place called Zitnic, near Sibenik. But we'll talk about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Slobodan Avlijas in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Avlijas on the road to Banja Luka where we were supposed to have a meeting in the Bosna Hotel in connection with the exchange of those people who were in the camp at Manjaca. We happened to meet on the road while we were waiting in line to pass through an area that was constantly under fire from the Muslim forces, especially sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when that was, what month in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I know it was in the second half of October. It may have been the 20th or the 22nd of October, 1992. We were supposed to meet in hotel Bosna, to discuss the further work of the commission, of the then-ARK Krajina, concerning the exchange of war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he ever appointed a member or did he ever do any work with your exchange commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He was an employee of the Ministry of Justice, although, for a long time -- although he had held that post for a long time and knew many people, Mr. Momcilo Mandic proposed that he go with me and the commission from Banja Luka to conduct that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That Mr. Avlijas go with you as a -- as a commissioner on the Central Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know a couple of inspectors at the MUP in 1992, named Goran Saric and Mirko Erkic. Did you know either one of those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
