utterances.text: Goran Saric. Maybe it's Saric with an S, yes. I did know him, yes. And I also knew Mr. Mirko Erkic who had worked in the Ministry of the Interior of ex-Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could show you, briefly, a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's P193. It's at tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is -- I don't know if you've seen this one before, Mr. Markovic. It's a document dated the 9th of August, 1992, and signed by the prime minister -- or for the prime minister by the deputy prime minister, Mr. Dubojevic [phoen]. And it's entitled: "A Decision on Forming Commissions for Visits to Collective Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoners." And you'll see that Mr. Avlijas, Mr. Saric, Mr. Erkic, and a Vojin Lale were named to commissions to visit and inquire into the status of persons situated in those facilities. Did you know about that? And this 9th of August is just a few days after there was a big international furor after some international reports went and took pictures at Manjaca, Omarska. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this decision on forming commissions for visits to collective centres. These centres and prisons were now under the Ministry of Justice. I know these people, but I never knew of the existence of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the -- the public outcry in the international press that took place a few days before this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We heard something about it. There were rumours. We were in the back of beyond as far as communications go. But it had to do with the camp at Manjaca [as interpreted] and that image that was doctored, showing this man behind the wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you, Were you aware that there were still --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. It's line 14 in transcript. It said "Manjaca," but I think witness said another name. It's Manjaca in line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It should be corrected, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you say something other than Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in my last answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that had to do with that camp, I think it was Omarska, where you see a thin person behind a wire and the others around him are walking around, sitting down, and this was represented as a terrible camp of the persons lounging around and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that as late as middle of November, 1992, there apparently were still some illegal camps and assembly centres in the Republika Srpska? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I knew that there were camps on the other side, even private camps in houses established by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Were you aware there were apparently still some illegal camps and assembly centres in the Republika Srpska as late as the middle of November 1992? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I knew about the legal camps - the collection centres, better to say - Manjaca, Kula, and Bileca, I think. As for the legal ones, those were the three. I didn't know about any illegal camps, and I personally doubt the existence of illegal camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Would the minister of justice be in a better position in November 1992 than you to know about whether such illegal camps and assembly centres existed? Would Mr. Mandic be in a better position?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, absolutely, yes, because all the camps were under his ministry. So he would have known. Because they were all under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: They had powers over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you one last exhibit, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's P253. It's at tab 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I can give you a hard copy with help from the usher. Coming to you in a minute, Mr. Markovic, is this exhibit. It's dated 17 November 1992, and it's the minutes of the 57th Session of the RS Government which had been held on 27 October. So I guess my question should be the end of October instead of the 17th of November. If you can turn to page 6 in the B/C/S, and it's page 6 of the English as well. I want to ask you about item number 22, Momcilo Mandic, ministry of judiciary and administration, has informed the government on the situation in Republika Srpska camps and assembly centres. "It is concluded that the existing illegal camps and assembly centres are to be dissolved as soon as possible." The way I read that means that at the time Mr. Mandic is saying this on, I guess, the 27th of October - I'm sorry, I misspoke before - there were still existing illegal camps and assembly centres in the Republika Srpska. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of them. And I have just said that only Justice Minister Momcilo Mandic was in the position to know. I myself did not know about them. Because all the camps, all the prisons were under the control and within the remit of the justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But when you were doing your work as a member of the commission and meeting with Mr. Masovic, he gave you a list of non-Serbs detained in Republika Srpska. Did he not indicate to you the suspected locations of where some of these detained persons were so you could look for them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He spoke about the locations, but Kula was mentioned most often. And we asked him to effect the exchange of prisoners from the military barracks, Viktor Bubanj and the central prison in Sarajevo, and today the barracks houses the supreme court, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markovic. I don't have any other questions for you at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, in addition to the caution that I would have given you earlier about slowing down, inasmuch as the cross-examination would be conducted by counsel who speaks the same language that you do, please remember to allow for a gap between the question to be completed by counsel and before you attempt to answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will try and do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I will try first follow the line of questioning pursued by my learned friend from the Prosecution, and I will start with the same topic as he did. Right at the beginning, the Prosecutor asked you when and why you left the joint MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if I'm not mistaken you said that on 17th April, 1992, you had arrived in Vrace and that before you arrived there, the interethnic relations in the joint MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been disrupted and this had created an atmosphere of intolerance in which it was impossible to work together side by side? Did I paraphrase you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I said. Not that the relations were disturbed, but they were outside of the bounds of any kind of normal behaviour. Threats, insults, cursing, even physical assaults on us, people from other ethnic communities who worked in the same ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, it's stopped. Very well. Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P650. It's an exhibit. I would like it to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a document -- well, you can see from its title what it is all about. These are statements by policemen of Muslim nationalities about their removal from the Pale and Sokolac Public Security Stations. And now I would like us to go on to the next page so that we can see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like the second paragraph to be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, could you please read this. And then I will have some questions for you. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see, at the end of this paragraph, members of the station of Muslim ethnicity claim that the station chief told them that the fact that they had been removed from their posts was a counter-measure in response to what had happened to the Serb police officers in the police station in the Stari Grad municipality in Sarajevo. So now let me ask you, Are aware of this incident at Pale? And then we will move on to the Stari Grad Police Station. So were you aware of this incident in Pale? Just wait a little bit before answering.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would not call this an incident. The chief of the public security station at Pale, Mr. Malko Koroman, wanted, at all costs, to keep the Muslims working in the station. But he also wanted the Serb policemen to return to their jobs in the Stari Grad Police Station. He insisted on it. I spoke to the public security station commander in Pale, a Muslim, whose name was Malik Krivic. He was a colleague of mine; I had worked with him before. He told me that Malko had asked him -- Malko Koroman had asked him not to come to Pale anymore because of his personal safety but that he would continue receiving his salary as if he had continued working. This is what Malik Krivic, the commander of the police station at Pale, told me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Krivic tell you that Mr. Koroman had told him what they say here, that this was a counter-measure in response to what happened at the Stari Grad Police Staying and that they would be able to go back to their jobs if the Serbs would return to their jobs in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me that in so many words, but that's how I interpreted that. In the Stari Grad Police Station where I started my police career in 1987 as the deputy police commander, there was a single Serb working who remained working there. And then after a few days, Ismet Dahic, the commander of the Stari Grad Police Station, sent him home, instructing him not to come back to his job anymore, because from that time on it was to be and it was 100 per cent ethnically pure Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the commander who sent him home because it was not in the record?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the commander of the public security station in Stari Grad in Sarajevo. His name was Ismet Dahic. And the chief of the station was Enes Bezdrop.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: They were both Muslims; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to look at document 1D00-2736.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I will not ask you to read this document. Let me just read whether you are familiar with this letter sent by the members of the Stari Grad Public Security Station of Serb ethnicity. Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I actually read it myself in early March of 1992, that's the date indicated here, when, in the Security Services Centre, I received a visit from the ethnic Serbs working in that station. And as a former officer in charge of that station, I was asked to give them my opinion as to what they should do, because they couldn't go on going to work because of the terrible insults they received on a daily basis from their erstwhile colleagues; their colleagues, ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In this letter, they list all the problems that they face in their work, and you can see here that they speak about the disproportion in the quantity of arms, the involvement -- interference of the Green Berets in the work of the station, and a number of irregularities that actually pushed them to the fringe, pushed those ethnic Serbs on the fringe, that they could no longer work properly in this police station. And in the end - and let us now look at the last page of this document - they say that they refused to work there anymore, and they placed themselves at the disposal of the Sarajevo SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior. And that is still the joint SUP.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for the record, I think this one is already an exhibit, and we should just indicate it is Exhibit 1D132, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I neglected to mention that this is in fact 1D132.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Markovic, just tell me, What did you do? What did you tell your colleagues? Obviously you knew them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were all employees who worked under me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I made a recommendation to them that they should try and persevere, because it was still possible at that time that with some effort on the part of our leaders, the people in charge, for the joint MUP to continue in existence, just like as the joint Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now let us just move on to page where the signatures are so that you can confirm whether these are, indeed, those people that you knew. Do you recognise their signatures? So do you recognise the signatures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Definitely. Number 1 is Cedo Nogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to go through them. Just tell us whether you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, each and every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree that this event in the Stari Grad Police Station preceded the event at Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer be needing this document. And now let us move on to the topic which actually brought you here today. When my colleague from the Prosecution asked you a question, you said that you received your salary throughout this time-period from the Ministry of the Interior, and you explained by saying that in essence nobody knew how long this commission would work. All the expectations were that it would be in existence for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Nobody had any idea how long this commission would continue working and how long this whole madness - it's the only way to describe it - would last. I received my salary from the Ministry of the Interior as an inspector in a police department because the Ministry of the Interior is an integral part of the government, and all the ministries are paid for from the government budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since it is the state budget, then there was no need for this commission of yours to be established as a professional commission because it was paid from the same treasury; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But I am now interested in the second part that you have failed to explain for us. I am interested in your status, in terms of the organisation, the responsibilities, and whom did you report in your work. Whom were you accountable to for your work? That's what you did not explain.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As for my work and the work of the entire commission, since I was there on my own for most of the time, I reported solely to the prime minister who had appointed me to that position by his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In that period while you worked in the commission, were you duty-bound to file any formal or informal reports to the Ministry of the Interior about the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As I've already explained, my only obligation was to submit reports to the prime minister through the justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Zecevic intervened at one point, and perhaps this is the right time to -- for you to complete your answer. You did, but it was not recorded in the transcript. You said that you met Minister Stanisic a couple of times and --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that he only wanted to know about the work of your commission and that he orally conveyed to you some suggestions and also indicated to you that you were duty-bound to comply with the Geneva Conventions and other international obligations. I heard you say "although this was in effect under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the army. That's what you said. So could you please explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic told me that, because I was a representative of the ministry, to make sure that I do everything in line with the law. But everything was under the jurisdiction of the justice of defence -- or, rather, of the Ministry of Justice, because the army did a large number of exchanges, and it set up its own commission which was headed by Dragan Bulajic, Captain Bulajic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the speakers are kindly asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were asked whether you received any instructions regarding your work, and, if so, who gave you those instructions, and you answered that question. But now I would like us to go back to this decision appointing your commission. If we could look at the contents of this document. You only dealt with the composition, but I'm interested in the bottom part of this decision. I do apologise. I'm looking for this document. It's a Prosecution Exhibit. I can't seem to be able to find it here in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps my colleague Mr. Hannis might assist me here. P228 I'm told. Correction, 427.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you need a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. I just want to have it on our screen. So if you could assist me with the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the decision appointing members of the commission? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the right document. Could you please just give me the exhibit number. The decision appointing the commission for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the 1992 decision to form a Central Commission? It's P179.18. I have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Well, perhaps we could give the hard copy to the witness, and the rest of us will be able to follow it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's the photo copy. We said it was not a very good quality, but if you would care to look at the bottom part of this document below the composition. It appears that when your commission was established some general instructions for its work were already provided. You can see that the exchanges on the principle all for all is mentioned here. That is what you told us, complying with security requirements, and so on. So you will agree with me that in the decision itself the government already gave you some initial instructions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were shown another document signed by Mr. Tomo Kovac, if I'm not mistaken. And we will have to go back to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is P192.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You remember that document? You commented on a part shown to you by the Prosecutor. However, the gist of this document can be seen in the text that follows. Look at paragraph 3, please. And then go on reading until you reach the end of the document. And after that we will comment on it. Mr. Kovac is suggesting to the president of the republic and the prime minister, the top government officials, that the basic problem be solved, which is categorising persons so that it can be clearly defined who is in charge of what category. In paragraph 3, he discusses the category of prisoners of war and concludes that the military or civilian judiciary should be in charge of them. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this category did exist and that the competence mentioned by him, the competency was in fact the way he describes it? I'm referring to prisoners of war, military prisoners.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. Because prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, but my English translation at paragraph 3 says: "We mean civilians and that category of prisoners of war ..." So paragraph 3 also seems to be talking about civilians. And unless the original says something different in Serbian, I'd like that clarified on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read the introductory part. So these are prisoners of war who have committed crimes against the civilian population. That, at least, is clear. Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just read out the Serbian part? Because the way Mr. Cvijetic is phrasing it doesn't seem to comply with what I read in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read this whole passage.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: "A second problem, a much more important problem in the field is that people are not properly categorised in the facilities or collection centres. We mean prisoners of war, persons who committed crimes, and the civilian population. In the first category, prisoners of war, when it comes to their physical integrity, food, hygiene, and so on, after they are identified exclusive" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we'll come to that. So I take note of my learned friend's intervention. So Mr. Kovac is discussing three categories. The first category are military prisoners of war. And in this sentence he says that military or civilians organs of the judiciary have authority over those. In the next passage, he discusses the second category. And these are persons who have committed crimes. And he says that the judiciary and the police organs have authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then let's move on to page 3, please. Next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, it's a little past time for the usual break. Would it be convenient to stop at this point and resume? Yes. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, on the last page of this document, Mr. Kovac deals with the third category of persons, that is, the civilian population. And you can see that he says here that as regards the accommodation of these persons, it's charities, NGOs that have to deal with these persons, and the local authorities, that they have to be provided with the minimum conditions. And that if they want to leave the area, they should be able to do so. I think you said that one of the main reasons why your commission was established was to ensure the free movement of civilians. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. That was one of the tasks of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the next passage, Mr. Kovac goes on to put forward his opinion, that all these categorise of persons should be treated according to the requirements of the international institutions, regardless of the manner in which the opposite side treats the Serbian population. I think you spoke about this, that you said that your work was based on humanitarian principles and international law. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. In this document, in the first paragraph, the second sentence, it says that civilians can only be given refugee status. They are not prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The last thing to which I wish to draw your attention in this document is on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we see that Mr. Kovac's observations contained in this document were forwarded to the president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the prime minister of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will agree with me that the president of Republika Srpska as the commander-in-chief is authorised to deal with all these categorise of persons, but especially as the commander-in-chief he is authorised to deal with the categorise of prisoners of war and issues of their accommodation and treatment, and that this document was send to the right address, as far as this area is concerned. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, sir. Because if anyone held the status, it was the president of the republic. So the document was really sent to the right people: The president of the republic, and the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have anticipated the second part of my question. The government was also authorised to deal with all the categorise of persons mentioned here and all these issues, as shown by the establishment of your commission by the government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The government implemented its orders through the Ministry of Justice, which was, in a manner of speaking, superior to this commission. It was its superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have now dealt with the evidence put to you by my learned friend. Now I'll show you several exhibits and documents dealing with these three categories of persons and the way they were taken carry of and accommodated in certain facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have on the screen 65 ter 1396, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a decision on the establishment of penitentiary-re-education institutions in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on page 2 -- can we go on to page 2 so we can see who issued this decision. Let's see the signature at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The then-acting -- those acting for the president, Presidency members, Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... think this is an exhibit already in evidence. It's 1D164.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I omitted to mention this. It is, in fact, 1D164.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you, as a policeman, were familiar with the fact that, on the territory of Republika Srpska there are penitentiary re-education facilities which existed before the war, during the war, and which still exist today, after the war?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We will have to divide them into two subcategories, and I will ask you to confirm what I say. In the seat of every district court, there was and still is a district prison which has a remand unit where persons on trial are inmates. And then there is another part where persons who have been sentenced to a prison sentence, not very high prison sentences, serve their sentence. Are aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This principle existed before the war, even during the war, and it still exists. All district courts have a district prison with these two categories of inmates that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You should be aware that the conditions and the way re -- detention on remand or the serving of prison sentences are implemented are under the authority of the president of the district court. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The second subcategory of these institutions are penitentiary re-education organisations where persons sentenced to long prison sentences serve their sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the wardens and their deputies are appointed exclusively by the minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said "minister."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Justice deal with both types of institutions, district prisons and penitentiary re-education organisations, and within the Ministry of Justice there is even an administrative officer dealing exclusively with these issues. He is in charge -- he or she is in charge of implementing prison sentences. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's actually not an administrative officer but an assistant minister for the execution of sanctions, or prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right; I was wrong. And let's clarify this. Both types of institutions have their own security service, the uniformed and armed prison police; is that right? Or, rather, prison guards, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. They wear blue uniforms, like the police, but they have different insignia on their sleeves. On these insignias, it says "judiciary police" or the name of the institution in which they work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to a specific institution of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's look at 1D03-4449.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, you are certainly aware of the fact that one of these penal and correctional institutions was Butmir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the remand prison or prison in Vogosca was, in fact, a department of the institution in Butmir? That stems from this document, but I'm asking you about your personal knowledge of this.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that before the war there was a prison called Butmir. It was, in fact, a detention unit of the semi-open type. As for its being a department in Vogosca, I really don't know about that. It was all within the competence of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you don't know, I'll move on. The document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have an objection about the document. I guess it's not being tendered yet, but there's no date on it either, so I don't know if it's relevant if we can't tie it to the relevant time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't tendering this document, so I don't think that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if he's not tendering it, then he shouldn't say it speaks for itself. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have 65 ter 1395.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this may be a response to my learned friend's objection. And on the 65 ter list we have the official document which shows that there was a department or a prison in Vogosca and that it belonged to the Ministry of Justice, and I only want to ask the witness whether he is aware that a private house was being used for the needs of this department. And the first and last name of the owner are mentioned in this document. Did you ever hear about the building called Planjina Kuca, as mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard of this decision, and I never heard -- I didn't know about this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would indicate for the record this is also an exhibit in evidence, P1327, and it can be speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the Prosecution, and, in fact, this is by way of explanation of my previous document to the effect that there was an official prison in Vogosca and that in the Vogosca department there was a private house where a department of that prison was set up, all within the Ministry of Justice. And this is relevant because Planjo's House, Planjina Kuca, was mentioned quite often by previous witnesses. But apparently we cannot pursue this topic any further with this witness, so I propose that we move on to our next document, and that is 1D03-4451.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, here we have a document issued by the municipality of Sokolac where they respond to the Ministry of Justice to their request that one of the buildings in the territory of that municipality be turned into an investigation centre or remand prison. And now I'm asking you whether can you conclude, based on this text, what this building was? Can you do that, since are you from that area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where this building is, but I heard that people were considering setting up this kind of facility in Sokolac. But I really don't know where it was because there were quite a few Muslim villages around Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can conclude, based on your answer, that this is a health care facility of some sort.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the minister of justice obviously did not have enough space and was looking for appropriate solutions where to put some categories of persons under the jurisdiction of the ministry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what happened. Because all official prisons were quite far away from Sokolac, and it was difficult to get to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. These were documents from the minister of justice. Now I'm going to show you a document from our 65 ter list, 1531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, on the previous document, I read we can -- in the transcript: "We can conclude, based on your answer, that this is a health care facility of some sort." Unless something is missing in the translation or in the transcript, I couldn't see that. It isn't -- it -- it could eventually be concluded when reading the document but not by hearing the answer of the witness. Did we miss something in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I followed your instructions. I said based on the text of the response to the ministry one can conclude that this was a health care facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then there was problem in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had the same thought, but then I read the answer carefully. And at page 66, line 23, it says, Well, I don't know where this -- The answer was: Well, I don't know where this building is, but I heard that people were building -- were considering setting up this kind of facility in Sokolac. So I thought maybe that was a reference to the document itself where it says something about a medical facility, and so I didn't object, but I think your point is well taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we have seen how the Minister of Justice worked formally, so to speak, on setting up this kind of institutions. But here we have an order from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vogosca where they issue a direct order to the prison warden to release 46 people, giving precise instructions as to how this is to be done. So I'm asking you whether your commission did come across of this kind of interference on the part of local authorities, Crisis Staffs, Presidencies, local or municipal and so on, in your work, because you will agree with me that under the rules and regulations, it was the justice ministry that was supposed to decide on the fate of those prisoners. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. And what they did infringed on the jurisdiction of the commission, whose member I was. But many municipalities in the field, on the ground, had their own Crisis Staffs, and those Crisis Staffs were the Alpha and Omega of the work of the entire municipality. As you can see from this document, the Crisis Staff issued an order. I'm referring to the Crisis Staff of the Vogosca municipality. So they were in a position to effect exchanges themselves bypassing the official State Commission for Exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You obviously are unaware of this document, this order. This is the first time that you've read it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. This is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when we're talking about the Ministry of Justice and these facilities, let me conclude by using another document from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is 65 ter 1402. And it is an exhibit too, P1318.22.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, I will give you some time to familiarise yourself with the document, and then I'm going to ask you some questions about it. This is a document from 1994, but it deals with the issue that covered one -- 1991 and 1992 and that is the admission of Muslim civilians in the Butmir correctional and penitentiary facility, penal and correctional facility. So we come to the third category of persons that we discussed, the category of refugees. You will agree with me that the fact that they were housed in this institution did not affect their status, because they were not prisoners of war and they were not convicts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the case. The document is dated the 28th of October, 1994. I was already working in the MUP by that time, and I was no longer a member of the commission. They were not considered as prisoners of war. But they were considered as refugees that had to be forwarded in order to achieve the re-unification of family or to achieve freedom of movement, to allow them to go wherever they want to go. And here it says that Captain Dragan Bulajic was the president of the Central Commission. We mentioned him as a representative of the Republika Srpska army doing the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The only reason why I called up this document is to try to show that sometimes it was not easy to categorise persons and, in particular, to find appropriate accommodation for each category. Practically here, they were put in an official penal institution and their status was that of refugees and they were put there only because they had to be housed somewhere. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Because they were in transit, in fact, if I may call it that. They were passing through the Serb territory with a destination in the Muslim territory, and they were treated as refugees, but they were housed in a penal and correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. This completes the line of questioning dealing with one type of a facilities where people were detained, and now I will move on to the next type of such facilities and another category of persons; the first category from the report that we read.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P61.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a document issued by Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic in which he orders the corps - you can see that in item 2 - to set up appropriate facilities in which to keep the first category of persons, i.e., prisoners of war, also specifying the conditions in line with international conventions. And also, which is of interest to us now here, is contained in item number 3 where he orders that the corps command shall independently set up prisoner exchanges, providing instructions as to how this is to be done. Can you see this from this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in the document, but I trust this had to do only with the prisoners of war held by either the Republika Srpska army or the BH army, so it's only logical for commissions to -- established in the army to do the exchanges because a single Central Commission could not deal with the civilians, the soldiers, and refugees and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, this was the essence of my question. In other words, did you know that the army commissions for exchange of prisoners were working parallel to your commission?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that only later when I met Captain Dragan Bulajic who had an office in Grbavica, in Sarajevo, and another office in Lukavica in the barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we can see how the army dealt with this issue. And now let us look at how the Supreme Command or the Supreme Commander dealt with this issue, at least when it comes to this kind of -- this category of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please look at 65 ter 2079, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the very bottom of this page of this Official Gazette, you can see the order. Yes. Right-hand side, bottom of the page, "order."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the application of the rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order on the application of the Rules of International Law of War in the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And can we then move on to the next page of this Official Gazette where it was published. And let us look at item 2. The president of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Radovan Karadzic says that: As for the application of the Rules of International Law of War, the commanders in the army are -- shall be responsible for this application and all other members of the army or the armed forces taking part in the armed -- in combat. So you will agree with me that this document is related to the previous document issued by General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in point 3, the minister of defence is authorised to prescribe the -- or, rather, to draw up the instructions on how prisoners should be treated. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. As this is an exhibit, we can now look at P189, and we can see the instructions drawn up by the minister. You know that Mr. Subotic was the minister of defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here, the rights and obligations of military personnel in categorising and looking after prisoners are described in details -- in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we go on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It deals with issues of camps and so on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the authorised body dealing with these issues was the president or Presidency of the republic, as we have already seen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But the issue of civilians, and I told you this in the preamble to one of my questions, was something that was dealt with by the Presidency as a state organ, not as Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's P587.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Here you can see an order issued by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see the text very well. It's very dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the technical staff to help you. There you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to point 3. The president here is dealing with the issue you mentioned and that is the free movement of civilians. So this order contains the basis for work on the free movement of civilians even by your commission, even though your commission was appointed by the government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll show you some minutes from a session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska dated the 9th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P179.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think it's paragraph 5, beginning with the words: "There has been no exchange of prisoners ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you read it to the end? You don't have to read it aloud; just read it silently to yourself. So my question is the following: Answering a question put to you by the Prosecutor, you said that the minister of justice was authorised to negotiate exchanges on his own. And here we see that the Presidency also dealt with a specific -- a particular exchange. So evidently this was a problem which occupied state organs such as the Presidency and the government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you what exchange this was about, what particular exchange; if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The minutes are dated the 9th of October, but I really don't know what this refers to. I can tell you that very often the opposite side, instead of bringing the people we asked for on our lists, would bring along children, elderly people, women, only to satisfy the number of people to be exchanged that was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So I have now concluded with this topic, the activities of the president and the Presidency, as regards exchanges and the treatment of these three categories of persons. And now I would like to move on to a set of documents issued by the Government of Republika Srpska in order to show the way in which the government dealt with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now have P200. 2-0-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You see that this refers to a government session of the 29th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Serbian version, please. Yes, thank you. And can we move on to the next page and look at point 7 and 8. 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, this is a situation you discussed with the Prosecutor when Mr. Vanovac was appointed because here under point 7 under the seventh item on the agenda we see that the proposal for appointing a president to the Central Commission for the Exchange of War Prisoners was on the agenda, as well as agreement on the conditions and way of exchanging war prisoners. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To see what this is about, we have to find the discussion, what was said about these items on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the ERN number because ... it's 0124-5452. It's page 6 in e-court I've just been told.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have received assistance. It's on page 6 of the same document. Yes, here we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Markovic, we now have the reply to the question of when Mr. Vanovac was appointed and how. So here we see that the minister of justice proposed him.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you say that he turned up, that he introduced himself to you. But it seems that he arrived before his appointment. Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came to Pale once and said that he had been appointed president of the Central Commission by the Ministry of Justice, or on behalf of the Ministry of Justice -- or, rather, that he had been appointed by Momcilo Mandic, the then-minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Some 20 days, or maybe a month later, he came again, and he showed me a document and even asked me to hand over the seal of the Central Commission, the stamp, which he took to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you something else about this document. In item 8, there's mention of an agreement on the conditions and way of exchange of prisoners. Do you know what this refers to? Was there such agreement, and did you implement it in your work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I think this was an agreement that war prisoners should be exchanged for war prisoners only on condition that the number of men should be equal. I think there's also mention of the wounded on both sides, as well as the exchange of bodies of fighters killed on both side. I think. I saw an agreement like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will show you one from the Prosecution set of exhibits and then one from the Defence set of exhibits. So, first, I'll show you P1427.23 [as interpreted]. It's P427 - not 1427 - .23. Please read this document through and then I'll ask you questions about it. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not the document I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll show you the one I think you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I have never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you just read in the text, it says that: In this agreement, the signatories established certain principles as to how exchanges were to be carried out, and they resemble the principles from the government decision on the appointment of your commission. Do you agree with what I've just said? Just look at the principles once again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These were the same principles that were mentioned in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your work, you adhered to these principles, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't find this other document, so I will now deal with another topic for the remainder of our time today. And that is the issue that I raised with the document from Vogosca, the fact that various Crisis Staffs and local authorities, local Presidencies, were involved in the exchanges of prisoners, the release of those prisoners. So now I would like to show you document 1D167. You can see here that the Crisis Staff of the municipality, you can see that that's the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Decides for all intents and purposes the fate of these people and in the items that follow categorises the persons who are to be released from imprisonment. You will agree with me that this looks very much like what we saw in Vogosca, what the War Commission issued there, again, the Crisis Staff, a local authority, decides on the fate of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. It's the exact same cases we saw in the case of the Vogosca municipality where the Crisis Staff issues a decision to release the prisoners and detainees. But this is dated the 2nd of June, 1992, and we couldn't get to Prijedor. We couldn't even fly there from Pale. All the roads were blocked, so it was really impossible to get to Prijedor and to do anything about that, to hold any kind of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you, in fact, anticipated what I was going to ask you. And that's precisely whether you were able to follow all these events throughout the territory of Bosnia -- or, rather, of Republika Srpska? Now that you've raised this issue, in what parts of Republika Srpska were you able to know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was able to see directly what was going on in the Sarajevo region, because there were roads there, although there were sniper incidents, but it was only in October that I reached Banja Luka, in late October. My presence was requested by the Croat commission because we wanted to effect an exchange in Zitnic, a place between Knin and Sibenik, the Croat and Serb prisoners were to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: From this category, I will show you just P1494; it's an exhibit. We're back in the municipality of Vogosca. And what I find interesting in this document is that it is headed the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, and you can see that it has a department for justice administration and regulations. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm looking at it, and I'm marvelling how a municipality can have a department for justice administration and regulations. As far as I know, no municipalities had courts, basic courts, any other judicial organs of that kind. I mean, not the municipality, but -- as a territorial unit, but the Municipal Assembly as a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely why I showed you this document, because this department again decides on the fate of the detained persons, and they're listed here by name, and it is doing your job, job -- the job of your commission.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, it was our job. Absolutely it was our job. And we were supposed to do that. But you can see this, that the Crisis Staff did that. In fact, it was their justice department of theirs. It was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we can perhaps finish with a statement. I think that this question was asked already. Obviously your commission had problems in its work. In order to be able to function as it was supposed to, as stipulated by the decision to establish it, it encountered problems of this sort.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, we had a lot of problems, primarily because the phone lines were down, and the provisions in the decision of the prime minister could not be complied with because of the war, and there was no communication whatsoever. And that was the only reason why we wanted to step down because we knew that -- or, rather, although we didn't know there were any such decisions of the -- this justice department of the Vogosca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, we are now in your neighbourhood. Can you tell us how far in the territory of the municipality of Sarajevo or Pale, where you were -- or, rather, can you describe the area which was out of your bounds, which could you not reach in the municipality of Sarajevo and Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb territory was very small. It was confined to Pale, although --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. It appears that my question was not recorded in the transcript -- or, rather, it appears that your answer was not recorded right from the beginning. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the Serb territory in Pale was very small, although the Serb army held the area around Sarajevo while the city itself was under the control of the federal part of Bosnia. All we could do was to meet at the demarcation line between the municipalities of Pale and Stari Grad and to conduct the exchanges of both prisoners of war and also to ensure the freedom of movement of the civilians who wanted to leave Sarajevo and go to Pale while it was still possible to do that, because, later on, Serbs no longer could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My specific question for you is: Were you able to communicate physically with Ilidza or, for instance, Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No way, we could not. We were able to have some kind of contact, limited contact with Ilidza perhaps for the first few days before the telephone lines were completely destroyed. And, for instance, in Lukavica, where I went to attend meetings with Amor Masovic, in a SFOR, IFOR, or whatever it was, APC, we travelled through paths in the woods that had been cleared recently, and -- to get there, to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just complete your answer regarding Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what to say about Trebinje? It's in the far south of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that did you not have any physical communication with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No way, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am observing the time, and I would like to show the witness just a few documents on a slightly different topic, so perhaps I should not now embark on that. So unless you're opposed and unless the Prosecution is opposed, perhaps we can finish for today and then continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Cvijetic. Mr. Markovic, we are about to take the adjournment for today. You, having been sworn as a witness, I am to remind you that you cannot have any communication whatever with counsel from either side in this matter; and, moreover, in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we adjourn now, to resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
